summary: Sirach 31 moves from the unrest caused by wealth to the rare praise of a rich person who does not go after gold. It then gives detailed counsel for meals: avoid greed at a shared table, receive food with restraint, be generous rather than stingy, and treat wine as good only when used in moderation.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Sirach’s wisdom at work in ordinary social settings: money, appetite, hospitality, and public behavior. It treats character as something revealed not only in worship or study, but also at the table.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the book into Greek.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with Jewish scribal learning, temple worship, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture in the background.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in compact poetic sayings and direct advice for ordinary conduct.

outline.heading: Wealth can steal rest
outline.note: Rich and poor alike toil, but the chapter opens by emphasizing how riches bring wakefulness and anxiety.

outline.heading: Gold tests the person who has it
outline.note: Love of gold leads many to ruin, while the truly blessed rich person is the one who can transgress and does not.

outline.heading: How to sit at a great table
outline.note: The teacher warns against greed, grabbing, and ignoring others at a shared meal.

outline.heading: Moderation and health
outline.note: Restraint in eating is linked with sleep, clear wits, and rest, while excess brings pain.

outline.heading: Generosity and stinginess with food
outline.note: The host or giver is judged by how freely or stingily food is shared.

outline.heading: Wine and self-control
outline.note: Wine can bring gladness when used in season and moderation, but excess exposes pride, conflict, and harm.

keyVerses.text: He who loves gold won’t be justified. He who follows destruction will himself have his fill of it.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the chapter’s warning about wealth most directly: the danger is not having resources, but loving and pursuing gold destructively.

keyVerses.text: Blessed is the rich person who is found blameless, and who doesn’t go after gold.
keyVerses.why: The chapter does not condemn every rich person. It singles out the rare person whose wealth has not captured their conduct.

keyVerses.text: Consider your neighbor’s feelings by your own. Be discreet in every point.
keyVerses.why: This is the center of the table counsel: manners are not just etiquette, but attention to the other person.

keyVerses.text: Wine drunk in season and in moderation is joy of heart and gladness of soul:
keyVerses.why: The chapter’s teaching on wine is balanced; it praises fitting use before warning against excess.

themes: gold as a test of character

questions.question: Is this chapter saying wealth is always bad?
questions.answer: No. The chapter warns that riches can bring wakefulness, anxiety, and moral danger, especially when a person loves gold or goes after it. But it also says a rich person can be called blessed if found blameless and not ruled by gold.

questions.question: Why does the chapter talk so much about sleep?
questions.answer: Sleep functions as a test of whether desire has become restless. Riches can take away sleep, illness can break it, and overeating can disturb it. Moderate eating is associated with healthy sleep and clear wits.

questions.question: What does “gold” represent here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, “gold” names wealth as an object of desire and pursuit. The warning is aimed at loving it, going after it, and letting it become a stumbling block. The text does not give a full economic theory; it gives moral instruction about what wealth can do to a person.

questions.question: What is difficult about verse 10?
questions.answer: Verse 10 praises the person who had the power to do wrong but did not. Readers may differ over whether this mainly describes temptation by wealth, public power, or opportunity in general. In the immediate chapter, the closest setting is wealth, because verses 5-11 are about gold, prosperity, and alms.

questions.question: Why does table behavior matter so much?
questions.answer: For this chapter, shared meals reveal whether a person is governed by appetite or by consideration for others. The advice is concrete: do not stare greedily, reach wherever desire points, eat greedily, or push ahead of others. The point is social wisdom, not merely polished manners.

questions.question: What does “Consider your neighbor’s feelings by your own” mean?
questions.answer: The saying asks the reader to use self-knowledge as a guide for treating another person. If one would dislike being crowded, ignored, or embarrassed at a meal, one should not do that to someone else. The surrounding verses apply that principle to eating in company.

questions.question: Is the chapter against wine?
questions.answer: No. It warns against showing off in wine and says wine has destroyed many, but it also calls wine in moderation “joy of heart and gladness of soul.” The contrast is between fitting, moderate use and excessive drinking that brings bitterness, conflict, rage, weakness, and wounds.

questions.question: Why should someone not rebuke a neighbor at a banquet of wine?
questions.answer: The final verse focuses on timing and setting. A banquet with wine is not the place to shame, reproach, or pressure someone. The chapter’s larger concern is that appetite, pride, and speech can turn a shared table into a place of conflict.

glossary.def: Sleeplessness or being kept awake; in this chapter it is linked with anxiety over riches and with physical distress.
A concrete word for wealth that can become an object of love, pursuit, and temptation.
A large or important meal setting where abundance can expose greed or restraint.
An image for desire that keeps looking for more and pulls the body toward excess.
Measured restraint; the chapter uses it especially for eating and drinking wine.
A festive meal with wine, where the teacher warns against rebuke, contempt, reproach, and making demands.
